subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Drawing Geometric Shapes with Given Conditions
intro: Eight multiple-choice questions on drawing and classifying triangles from given conditions: the triangle inequality, the $180^\circ$ angle sum, and the congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS) versus the AAA and ambiguous SSA cases.

items.prompt:
Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $4\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$, and $11\text{ cm}$?
A) Yes, because all three lengths are positive.
B) No, because $4 + 5 = 9 < 11$.
C) Yes, because $5 + 11 > 4$.
D) No, because the sides are all different lengths.

steps: Apply the triangle inequality: the sum of the two shorter sides must be greater than the longest side.
The two shorter sides are $4$ and $5$, and the longest side is $11$. Check $4 + 5 = 9$.
Since $9 < 11$, the two shorter sides cannot reach across the longest side, so no triangle exists. Answer B is correct.

A is wrong: positive lengths alone do not guarantee a triangle. C is wrong: it tests the longest side plus a short side ($5 + 11 > 4$) instead of the two shortest sides. D is wrong: triangles can have three different side lengths (scalene).

items.prompt:
Can a triangle have interior angles measuring $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$?
A) No, because the angles sum to $190^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.
B) Yes, because the angles are all different.
C) Yes, because the angles could sum to $360^\circ$ overall.
D) No, because a triangle cannot contain a $90^\circ$ angle.
items.answer: A) No, because the angles sum to $190^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.

steps: The three interior angles of any triangle must sum to exactly $180^\circ$.
Add the given angles: $40 + 60 + 90 = 190$.
Since $190^\circ \ne 180^\circ$, no triangle has these angles. Answer A is correct.

B is wrong: distinct angles do not guarantee a valid sum. C is wrong: $360^\circ$ is the angle sum of a quadrilateral, not a triangle. D is wrong: a right triangle has a $90^\circ$ angle, so that is allowed.
solution.answer: A) No, because the angles sum to $190^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.

items.prompt:
Which set of three side lengths CAN form a triangle?
A) $3\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$
B) $2\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}$, $9\text{ cm}$
C) $6\text{ cm}$, $8\text{ cm}$, $10\text{ cm}$
D) $1\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$, $9\text{ cm}$

steps: A triangle is possible only when the two shorter sides sum to MORE than the longest side.
For C: $6 + 8 = 14 > 10$, so a triangle can be formed. Answer C is correct.
A is wrong: $3 + 4 = 7$, which equals the longest side, so it collapses into a straight segment (degenerate, no triangle).
B is wrong: $2 + 2 = 4 < 9$. D is wrong: $1 + 5 = 6 < 9$. Both fail the triangle inequality.

items.prompt:
A triangle is described by two sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $40^\circ$ between them. How many triangles satisfy these conditions, and which criterion applies?
A) More than one triangle; AAA
B) Exactly one triangle; SAS
C) No triangle; the sides are too short
D) Exactly one triangle; SSS

steps: Two sides and the angle BETWEEN them are given. This is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) configuration.
SAS fixes the two sides and the angle between them, so the third side and the figure are completely determined: exactly one triangle (up to congruence). Answer B is correct.

A is wrong: AAA needs three angles and gives infinitely many similar triangles, not this case. C is wrong: SAS always produces a valid triangle. D is wrong: SSS requires all three side lengths, but here an angle is given instead of the third side.

items.prompt:
Conditions: a triangle has interior angles of $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $70^\circ$, with no side length given. How many triangles meet these conditions?
A) Exactly one triangle, because the angles are fixed.
B) No triangle, because the angles do not sum to $180^\circ$.
C) More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes).
D) Exactly one triangle, by the SSS criterion.
items.answer: C) More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes).

steps: First check feasibility: $50 + 60 + 70 = 180^\circ$, so the angles are valid for a triangle.
Only the three angles are given (the AAA case). Angles fix the shape but not the size.
With no side length to set the scale, you can draw infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes, so more than one triangle exists. Answer C is correct.
A is wrong: angles alone do not fix size. B is wrong: the angles do sum to $180^\circ$. D is wrong: SSS requires three sides, none are given here.
solution.answer: C) More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes).

items.prompt:
Using a ruler and protractor, you draw a $7\text{ cm}$ base, then a $45^\circ$ angle at one end of the base and a $60^\circ$ angle at the other end, extending the two rays until they meet. How many triangles result, and which criterion applies?
A) Exactly one triangle; ASA
B) More than one triangle; AAA
C) No triangle; the angles are too small
D) Two triangles; the ambiguous SSA case

steps: A side (the $7\text{ cm}$ base) is given with the two angles at its endpoints. This is Angle-Side-Angle (ASA).
The two rays from the ends of the fixed base meet at exactly one point, so exactly one triangle is determined. Answer A is correct.

B is wrong: a side length is fixed, so this is ASA, not AAA, and the triangle is unique. C is wrong: $45 + 60 = 105^\circ < 180^\circ$, leaving a valid third angle of $75^\circ$. D is wrong: SSA needs two sides and a non-included angle, but here only one side is given.

items.prompt:
Two sides of a triangle measure $5\text{ cm}$ and $9\text{ cm}$. What is the range of possible lengths $c$ for the third side?
A) $5 < c < 9$
B) $4 < c < 14$
C) $c > 14$
D) $0 < c < 14$

steps: The third side $c$ must satisfy the triangle inequality with both given sides: $|a - b| < c < a + b$.
Compute the bounds with $a = 5$ and $b = 9$: $|5 - 9| = 4$ and $5 + 9 = 14$.
So the third side must satisfy $4 < c < 14$. Answer B is correct.

A is wrong: it just lists the two given sides as bounds. C is wrong: $c$ must be less than $14$, not greater. D is wrong: it omits the lower bound, allowing values like $c = 3$ for which $3 + 5 = 8 < 9$ fails.

items.prompt:
A triangle has one angle of $35^\circ$ and another angle of $85^\circ$, plus a side of $10\text{ cm}$ included between those two angles. How many triangles satisfy these conditions, and what is the third angle?
A) More than one triangle; third angle $60^\circ$
B) No triangle; the angles exceed $180^\circ$
C) Exactly one triangle; third angle $60^\circ$
D) Two triangles (ambiguous SSA); third angle $60^\circ$
items.answer: C) Exactly one triangle; third angle $60^\circ$

steps: Find the third angle using the angle sum: $180 - 35 - 85 = 60^\circ$.
The given side lies between the two known angles, so this is the Angle-Side-Angle (ASA) configuration.
ASA determines a unique triangle, so exactly one triangle exists with a third angle of $60^\circ$. Answer C is correct.

A is wrong: a fixed included side makes the triangle unique (this is not AAA). B is wrong: $35 + 85 = 120^\circ < 180^\circ$, so the angles are valid. D is wrong: SSA needs two sides and a non-included angle, but here only one side is given, so there is no ambiguity.
solution.answer: C) Exactly one triangle; third angle $60^\circ$
